lessons.title: Discrete random variables and the Poisson distribution
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board — Advanced Level Mathematics, Statistics (Upper Sixth part; to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Calculate $E(X)$ and $\text{Var}(X)$ of a discrete random variable
Model rare events in time or space
reviewNotes: Poisson approximation to the binomial and sum of independent Poissons only briefly mentioned.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Discrete random variable
blocks.md: A discrete random variable $X$ with probabilities $p_i$ ($\sum p_i=1$): $E(X)=\sum x\,p$, $E(X^2)=\sum x^2p$ and $\text{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2$. Also $E(aX+b)=aE(X)+b$ and $\text{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\text{Var}(X)$.

blocks.title: Poisson distribution
blocks.md: $X\sim\text{Po}(\lambda)$ models the number of events in a fixed interval when events occur singly, independently, at a constant average rate. $P(X=r)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^r}{r!}$ for $r=0,1,2,s'$ Mean $=$ variance $=\lambda$. Over a longer interval multiply $\lambda$ (e.g. 2 hours: $2\lambda$).

blocks.title: Method
blocks.md: 1. Identify $\lambda$ for the interval asked. 2. Use $P(X=r)$ directly for exact values; for 'at least' use the complement: $P(X\geq k)=1-P(X\leq k-1)$. 3. State the answer to 3 or 4 decimal places.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md: Forgetting to rescale $\lambda$ when the interval changes. $P(X\geq1)=1-P(X=0)$, not $1-P(X=1)$. The Poisson model fails if events cluster or happen simultaneously.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: $X$ takes values 1, 2, 3, 4 with probabilities 0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2. Find $E(X)$ and $\text{Var}(X)$.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Calls to a call centre arrive at an average of 2.5 per minute ($\text{Po}(2.5)$). Find $P(X=0)$ and $P(X\geq2)$.

lessons.title: Hypothesis testing
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board — Advanced Level Mathematics, Statistics (Upper Sixth part; to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Carry out one-tailed and two-tailed tests for a binomial proportion and a normal mean
reviewNotes: Test for a Poisson mean and tests with unknown variance (t-test) not included.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Hypotheses and significance
blocks.md: The **null hypothesis** $H_0$ is the claim being tested (e.g. $p=0.5$ or $\mu=50$); the **alternative** $H_1$ says $p>0.5$ (one-tailed), $p<0.5$ (one-tailed) or $p\neq0.5$ (two-tailed). The **significance level** $\alpha$ (often 5%) is the probability of rejecting $H_0$ when it is true (a Type I error).

blocks.title: Binomial test
blocks.md: Assume $H_0$ and compute the probability of the observed result or more extreme under $B(n,p_0)$. If this probability is less than $\alpha$ (halve $\alpha$ for two-tailed), reject $H_0$. The **critical region** is the set of values leading to rejection.

blocks.title: Test for a normal mean
blocks.md: For a sample of size $n$ from a normal population with known $\sigma$, under $H_0$ the sample mean is $N\left(\mu_0,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)$. Test statistic $z=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$. Critical values: 5% one-tailed $\pm1.645$; 5% two-tailed $\pm1.96$.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md: Failing to reject $H_0$ does NOT prove $H_0$ true: there is insufficient evidence against it. Write conclusions in context (e.g. 'there is evidence that the mean mass is less than 50 kg'). Do not divide by $\sigma^2$ or forget $\sqrt n$.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: A coin is tossed 12 times and shows 10 heads. Test at 5% whether it is biased towards heads.
steps: $P(X\geq10)=\frac{66+12+1}{4096}=0.0193<0.05$: reject $H_0$; there is evidence of bias towards heads.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Bags of maize flour are labelled 50 kg with $\sigma=2$ kg. A sample of 25 has mean 49.2 kg. Test at 5% whether the mean is less than 50 kg.
blocks.answer: Reject $H_0$: evidence the mean is below 50 kg

lessons.title: Correlation and regression
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board — Advanced Level Mathematics, Statistics (Upper Sixth part; to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Calculate and interpret the product moment correlation coefficient $r$
Use the line for prediction and comment on its reliability
reviewNotes: Spearman's rank correlation and the regression of $x$ on $y$ are not included.
Scatter diagram line points are plotted by hand from the computed regression line.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Summary statistics and $r$
blocks.md: $S_{xx}=\sum(x-\bar x)^2$, $S_{yy}=\sum(y-\bar y)^2$, $S_{xy}=\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)$. The correlation coefficient $r=\frac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}}$ satisfies $-1\leq r\leq1$: near $+1$ strong positive, near $-1$ strong negative, near 0 no linear correlation.

blocks.title: Regression line of $y$ on $x$
blocks.md: $y=a+bx$ with gradient $b=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}$ and intercept $a=\bar y-b\bar x$. The line passes through $(\bar x,\bar y)$ and minimises the sum of squares of the vertical distances to the points. Use it to predict $y$ from $x$ (not $x$ from $y$).

blocks.title: Interpretation
blocks.md: Interpolation (predicting inside the range of the data) is reasonably reliable if $r$ is close to $\pm1$; extrapolation (outside the range) is not. Correlation does not imply causation: two variables may both depend on a third one.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md: Using the line of $y$ on $x$ to estimate $x$. Interpreting $r=0$ as 'no relationship' (there could be a non-linear one). Quoting $r$ with a value greater than 1 in magnitude means a calculation error.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: For $x=1,2,3,4,5$ and $y=2,4,5,4,5$ find $r$ and the regression line.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A shop records advertising spend $x$ (thousand FCFA) and sales $y$ (units): $(10,25),(20,38),(30,50),(40,66),(50,76)$. Find the regression line and predict sales at $x=35$.

exercises.prompt: Explain what a Type I error is, in the context of a 5% significance test of a new fertiliser.
exercises.model: A Type I error is rejecting the null hypothesis ('the fertiliser has no effect') when it is actually true, i.e. concluding the fertiliser works when it does not. At a 5% significance level the probability of this error is 5%.
